sections.b: After the Temple is rededicated, the revolt changes shape. Judas rescues Jews besieged in Gilead and Galilee (1 Maccabees 5). Antiochus IV dies in the east, and a royal army defeats Judas at Beth-zechariah, where his brother Eleazar dies under an elephant (1 Maccabees 6:1–47). Lysias then grants the Jews their own laws (1 Maccabees 6:59), the goal the revolt began with. The fight goes on against the high priest Alcimus and the general Nicanor, whose defeat on the thirteenth of Adar becomes a yearly feast (1 Maccabees 7). Judas then seeks a treaty with Rome (1 Maccabees 8).

sections.h: 1 Maccabees 5: the law of war applied again
sections.b: 1 Maccabees tells Judas's campaigns of 163 BC in the words of Israel's war law. He puts the sons of Baean under the ban (1 Maccabees 5:5), offers peace to Ephron before attacking it (1 Maccabees 5:48; Deuteronomy 20:10), kills every male at Bosor, Maapha and Ephron (1 Maccabees 5:28, 35, 51; Deuteronomy 20:13), and burns the idols of Azotus (1 Maccabees 5:68; Deuteronomy 7:5). No prophet commands these wars; the writer shows Judas keeping the written law. Christian teaching on noncombatants (Catechism 2313–2314) and Basil's advice that soldiers who had killed should keep from communion for a time judge the same acts more severely.

sections.b: By the second century BC the descendants of Esau held the land south of Judea, including Hebron, which the Greeks called Idumea. Judas fought them twice, at Akrabattene and in the south, where he destroyed Hebron's stronghold (1 Maccabees 5:3; 1 Maccabees 5:65). The royal army came "by way of Idumea" to attack Beth-zur (1 Maccabees 6:31). A generation later John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and made its people accept circumcision (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258); Herod the Great was of Idumean descent.

The earliest Jewish portrait of Rome is the praise in 1 Maccabees 8:1–16: mighty in war, loyal to its friends, ruled by a Senate with no king. Judas sends envoys, and Rome makes a treaty of mutual aid with the Jews, written on bronze (1 Maccabees 8:17–32), about 161 BC. The picture is far from that of Daniel's fourth beast (Daniel 7:7, 23) as most readers have taken it, and from Revelation's Babylon (Revelation 17). The difference is mostly one of date: 1 Maccabees was written before Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC.

At Beth-zechariah Eleazar, Judas's brother, "gave himself to save his people" by killing an elephant he thought carried the king, and was crushed when it fell (1 Maccabees 6:43–46). Ambrose praised him as a model of courage (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207), and Christian moralists have generally kept such deaths in battle apart from the suicide that Augustine forbade (City of God 1.21–26). Compare Samson (Judges 16:30) and Razis (2 Maccabees 14:37–46).

sections.h: Antiochus IV and the little horn
sections.b: 1 Maccabees 6 tells the death of Antiochus IV in Persia in 164 BC, grieving over what he did in Jerusalem. Many readers have taken him as the horn of Daniel 8 and the king of Daniel 11:21–35. Whether Daniel 7 and Daniel 11:36–45 also speak of him, or of a final Antichrist, divides the churches: Jerome and the Catholic tradition, the Orthodox fathers, Luther, Calvin, Adventist writers and dispensationalists give different answers, set out in the card on 1 Maccabees 6.

sections.h: Alcimus, high priest by royal appointment
sections.b: In 162 BC Demetrius I made Alcimus high priest and sent him to Judea with an army (1 Maccabees 7:5–9). He was a priest of Aaron's line, which is why the Hasideans trusted him; he killed sixty of them (1 Maccabees 7:12–16). His rule shows how far the high priesthood had come under foreign kings: an office granted by a pagan ruler and held by force. Later, Jonathan and Simon received the same office from Seleucid kings (1 Maccabees 10:20; 1 Maccabees 14:38).

Antiochus IV died in the east in 164 BC, naming Philip guardian of his son; Lysias made the boy king as Antiochus V Eupator (1 Maccabees 6:14–17). In 162 BC Demetrius I, son of Seleucus IV, escaped from Rome, where he had been a hostage, and had Antiochus V and Lysias killed (1 Maccabees 7:1–4). A Babylonian tablet (BM 35603) helps date these reigns. The quarrels within the house of Seleucus often decided what happened in Judea (1 Maccabees 6:55–63).

The defeat of Joseph and Azariah, who fought without Judas's leave, ends with the writer's moral: "They were not of the seed of those men by whose hand Israel was given salvation" (1 Maccabees 5:62). Many scholars read this verse as a key to the book's purpose, to show that God saved Israel through Mattathias's family. The same chapters tell the death of Judas's brother Eleazar (1 Maccabees 6:43–46) and Judas's treaty with Rome (1 Maccabees 8), which his brothers renewed.

sections.h: Nicanor's Day and the thirteenth of Adar
sections.b: Judas defeated Nicanor on the thirteenth of Adar, 161 BC, and the day became a yearly feast (1 Maccabees 7:43–49). It is the day on which the Jews' enemies in Esther had hoped to destroy them (Esther 9:1), and 2 Maccabees 15:36 places Nicanor's Day "the day before Mordecai's day". Later the thirteenth became the Fast of Esther, and Nicanor's Day was forgotten.

1 Maccabees adds a feast to Israel's year: the thirteenth of Adar, kept for the victory over Nicanor (1 Maccabees 7:49), as Hanukkah was kept for the rededication (1 Maccabees 4:59). Megillat Ta'anit, a first-century list of days on which fasting was forbidden, includes it, and both Talmuds remember it (Bavli Taanit 18b; Yerushalmi Taanit 2:12).

sections.h: A Sabbath year during the siege
sections.b: Beth-zur surrendered and the Temple's defenders ran short of food because "it was a Sabbath year for the land" (1 Maccabees 6:49, 53). The law left fields unsown every seventh year (Leviticus 25:1–7; Exodus 23:10–11), and these verses show it being kept in the 160s BC, at great cost. Josephus also mentions sabbath years in this period (Antiquities 12.378; 13.234).

When Alcimus killed sixty Hasideans, 1 Maccabees quoted Psalm 79:2–3 over them: the flesh and blood of God's loyal ones spilled around Jerusalem, with no one to bury them (1 Maccabees 7:16–17). The psalm's word for "loyal ones" is the Hasideans' own name. Later the priests' prayer against Nicanor (1 Maccabees 7:37–38) uses the lament's plea, "Remember".

1 Maccabees keeps two kinds of death apart. Those who die rather than break the law are martyrs (1 Maccabees 1:62–63; 1 Maccabees 2:29–38). Eleazar, who dies in battle killing an elephant (1 Maccabees 6:43–46), and the priests who fell "without thinking it through" (1 Maccabees 5:67) are not called martyrs. Christian writers such as Ambrose nevertheless set Eleazar beside the martyrs as an example of courage (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207–208).

Judas heard of Rome's power and loyalty to its friends (1 Maccabees 8:1–16) and sent Eupolemus and Jason to make friendship and an alliance, "to lift the yoke from them" (1 Maccabees 8:17–18). The Senate's reply, written on bronze, binds each side to help the other in war and to give nothing to the other's enemies, with a warning to Demetrius (1 Maccabees 8:23–32). The book approves without reserve. Rome sent no help when Bacchides came back and Judas fell (1 Maccabees 9:1–18), and 2 Maccabees never mentions the treaty, crediting God alone with Nicanor's defeat (2 Maccabees 15:21–27).

The report of Rome in 1 Maccabees 8 admires a people that has no king: "none of them wore a crown or dressed in purple to make himself great by it" (1 Maccabees 8:14), and a council of three hundred twenty that meets daily (1 Maccabees 8:15). The writer gets details wrong (Rome had two consuls, not one ruler, 1 Maccabees 8:16), and the praise is striking in a book written for readers whose Hasmonean rulers were high priests and, from about 104 BC, kings.
